issue.title: Care worker pay talks: who pays for the first Fair Pay Agreement?
issue.question: Care workers' pay will now be negotiated by unions and employers, backed by £500 million. Who should pay for any rise above that, and who should have the last word on the deal?
issue.summary: On 25 November 2026 the government named Baroness Christina McAnea to chair the new body that will negotiate care workers' pay, terms and conditions in England, covering about 1.5 million people. The first Fair Pay Agreement is backed by £500 million, talks start in April 2027 and the first settlement is due by April 2028. Councils will have a non-voting, advisory role, and the government sets the funding limit for each round. In 2024-25 frontline care workers earned on average 79p an hour above the minimum wage, according to Resolution Foundation analysis.
issue.slot_reason: Social care last came up on 12 November, and no field has waited longer with a UK story today. On 25 November the government named the chair who will lead care workers' pay talks, so the question of who pays is now live.

bench.title: Government pays the rise above £500m, tested in volunteer councils
bench.answer: Keep the talks and the chair. Change who carries the cost. Trial: in volunteer councils picked by lot, the Department of Health and Social Care pays any agreed rise above the £500 million, and publishes the cost before signing. Others get no less than today. Measured by 30 June 2029: care workers staying in their jobs, against places like it. Provisional fail: leavers fall by less than 2 in every 100, or a picked council cuts home care. Stops on 31 March 2030 unless Parliament votes to keep it. Passes, and it goes national. Leaves out Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland and non-volunteer councils. The Secretary of State signs it.

bench.title: Government pays the rise direct, not councils: a small trial
bench.answer: Take the bill off councils. In volunteer council areas picked by lot, government pays any rise agreed in the talks straight to care firms for wages. Councils don't find it, so council tax and local services aren't touched. Workers and employers still agree the deal; councils advise, as planned [s2]. Other areas get today's arrangement, never less. We compare pay with the 79p an hour above minimum wage seen in 2024-25 [s3]. Provisional fail line: under 50p more than comparison areas by April 2028. Stops on 30 April 2028 unless Parliament votes to keep it. Passes, and it goes national. Leaves out Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Signed by the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care.

bench.title: Let carers and care users sign off the extra pay
bench.answer: Your mum's care isn't a rounding error. Keep a national pay floor; trial extra pay through councils, with elected carers and care users jointly approving each local deal. Parliament funds rises above £500 million through a capped grant from general taxation, conditional on audited wages, unchanged fees and care hours. Draw twelve volunteer council areas by lot; others keep existing funding. Publish staff retention and delivered care hours quarterly. Provisional failure: retention improves under five percentage points against similar areas, or care hours fall. Funding stops in April 2029 unless Parliament renews it after review; success means national rollout. Count unpaid carers and self-funders separately: this won't cover everyone. Workers and users approve deals; Parliament approves spending.

rows.test: Test: government pays any rise, not councils or firms
rows.note: The Department of Health and Social Care would pay any agreed rise above £500m in the picked councils. Elsewhere today's arrangement stays. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Test: a proper wage that isn’t cut later
rows.note: It measures staying in the job, not the wage itself, and the funding would stop on 31 March 2030 unless Parliament keeps it. What counts as proper isn’t said.
It keeps the talks and chair, so the dates stay as announced: talks from April 2027, first settlement by April 2028. It neither speeds nor slows them.

rows.test: Limit: care homes and home care aren’t closed or cut
rows.note: Its fail line catches a picked council cutting home care. Nothing watches for care homes closing.

rows.test: Limit: council tax, rent and bills don’t go up
rows.note: Councils would pay nothing extra in the picked areas, so nothing here pushes council tax up. Fees to self-funders aren't mentioned. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Limit: no open-ended bill, a set limit and a review date
rows.note: It pays "any agreed rise" with no cap, so the bill has no set limit. The review date is there (31 March 2030). Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Test: government pays any rise, not councils or firms
rows.note: Government would pay any agreed rise straight to care firms in the picked areas, so councils and firms wouldn't find it. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Test: a proper wage that isn’t cut later
rows.note: It measures pay directly (50p more than comparison areas), but by April 2028, the month the first settlement is due. The funding would stop on 30 April 2028 unless Parliament keeps it.
It leaves the talks as planned: first settlement by April 2028. It neither speeds nor slows them.

rows.test: Limit: care homes and home care aren’t closed or cut
rows.note: Nothing in the answer measures care homes closing or care being cut. It only says local services wouldn’t be touched.

rows.test: Limit: council tax, rent and bills don’t go up
rows.note: It says council tax and local services aren't touched, because government pays direct. Fees to self-funders aren't mentioned. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Limit: no open-ended bill, a set limit and a review date
rows.note: It pays "any rise agreed" with no cap, so the bill has no set limit. The review date is there (30 April 2028). Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Test: government pays any rise, not councils or firms
rows.note: Parliament would fund rises above £500m through a capped grant. If a rise costs more than the cap, councils or firms could be left to find the rest.

rows.test: Test: a proper wage that isn’t cut later
rows.note: Funding is tied to audited wages, but the "national pay floor" is never defined, retention is what’s measured, and funding stops in April 2029 unless Parliament renews it.
It adds a local sign-off by elected carers and care users on each deal, with no deadline. That could slow the national talks or not. The answer doesn’t say.

rows.test: Limit: care homes and home care aren’t closed or cut
rows.note: Delivered care hours falling is a fail, and the grant is conditional on unchanged hours. Nothing watches for care homes closing.

rows.test: Limit: council tax, rent and bills don’t go up
rows.note: The money would come from a grant out of general taxation, conditional on unchanged fees, so councils and users would pay nothing extra. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

rows.test: Limit: no open-ended bill, a set limit and a review date
rows.note: The grant is capped and stops in April 2029 unless Parliament renews it. The cap's size isn't stated. Needs no source: it follows from what the answer says.

gate.verdict: None of the three passes every test and limit. A and B fail the limit on an open-ended bill; C passes it but leaves four tests unclear. The facts can’t settle who should pay for a rise above £500m, or who has the last word.
rejected_claims: summary: the Secretary of State sets the funding limit for each round (the source says central government agrees the limit and the Secretary of State’s remit letter carries it; reworded to "the government sets")

jury.question: Who should carry the cost of a pay rise above £500 million, and who should have the last word on the deal: taxpayers nationally, councils, or care workers and users?
options: National taxpayers pay in full, with a set cap and review date
Government pays, but only up to a fixed cap; the talks stay within it
Councils share the cost, with a say in the deal
Care workers and care users approve the deal, Parliament approves the money
jury.ruling: Government pays, but only up to a fixed cap; the talks stay within it. Four of the twelve chose it, the most of any option: it is the only one that keeps the bill capped while the talks stay inside it.

reasons.text: The government should pay, but with a ceiling written down. Otherwise the bill is open-ended and nobody can plan for it.
Care is a national job, so the nation should pay. But a cap and a review date are the sensible bit.
Councils know their areas and their care homes. Give them a real say and some of the bill, or they'll just be told.
The people who wash and feed my generation should be the ones signing off the deal, not a minister in London.

minister.trial: Before talks open in April 2027 the Department of Health and Social Care publishes one fixed cap on any rise above the £500m, and the talks stay inside it. In 12 volunteer English councils drawn by lot, the Department pays any rise within the cap straight to care firms. Councils pay nothing extra. 12 councils like them keep today's arrangement.
minister.fail_number: Provisional: fails if any of the 12 councils cuts home care or raises council tax to cover care, or if fewer than 2 more in 100 care workers stay than in the 12 like them, by 31 March 2029.
minister.statement:
Twelve simulated jurors, drawn by lot, voted 4 of 12 for this: government pays, up to a fixed cap, and the talks stay inside it. Three wanted councils to share the bill, three wanted care workers and users to approve the deal, two wanted the nation to pay in full.

I'm signing the four. 12 volunteer councils, drawn by lot, pay nothing extra. The trade-off is plain: a cap means the talks can't promise more than it holds.

Two answers on the bench had no cap. The gate failed them. A pay deal is not an open tab. Cap first, then the number.

predictions.claim: By 15 January 2027 the government publishes its adult social care workforce plan, which it said was due by the end of 2026.
predictions.rule: True if a GOV.UK page dated 27 November 2026 to 15 January 2027 publishes a workforce plan for adult social care in England. A press release only promising one does not count.

predictions.claim: By 30 April 2027 the first round of care worker pay talks has formally opened in England.
predictions.rule: True if GOV.UK or a news report dated by 30 April 2027 says the first formal negotiating meeting of the care workers' negotiating body has taken place. False otherwise.

predictions.claim: By 31 March 2027 the government announces total funding for the first care worker pay agreement of more than £500 million.
predictions.rule: True if a GOV.UK page or ministerial statement dated 27 November 2026 to 31 March 2027 gives a funding figure above £500 million for the first agreement. False otherwise.
